'''Tizer''' is an orange-coloured, citrus-flavoured carbonated [[soft drink]] bottled and sold in the UK. It was launched in 1924 by Fred and Tom Pickup when it was known as "Pickup's Appetizer", later abbreviated to Tizer.<ref name=Herald>{{cite news|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/default_content/12754924.forgotten-recipe-puts-fizz-back-tizer/|title=Forgotten recipe puts the fizz back into Tizer|date=27 January 2007|website=[[The Herald (Glasgow)|The Herald]]}}</ref> The original Tizer company would produce a range of other soft drinks including Jusoda. The drink has been manufactured by A.G. Barr since 1972.

==History==
=== Early history ===

Thomas Pickup was born on 21 July 1884 in Ashworth, Lancashire, while his brother Fred was born in 1879 in Heap, Birtle, Lancashire to parents Edmund Pickup and Eliza Saxon.<ref name=WC_Museum>{{cite web|url=http://westcountrybottles.co.uk/mike4/Companies/Bristol_Companies/Pickup.html|title=Pickup & Co|website=West Country Bottle Museum|access-date=28 April 2026}}</ref> Edmund's brother, Abraham, was by 1901 in partnership with Thomas Fentiman as ''Fentiman & Pickup'', botanical brewers based in Middlesbrough.<ref name=WC_Museum/> The partnership dissolved in 1903, when Fentiman retired, with Abraham continuing the business until his death in 1906, which at this time his widow Harriet continued the business.<ref name=WC_Museum/> By 1907, Thomas and Fred, along with their sister and mother had setup ''Pickup & Co'', as botanical brewers in Bristol, and by 1910 had opened a branch in Pontypridd.<ref name=WC_Museum/> A year later Fred had moved to Leeds, setting up ''F Pickup'', but in 1919, Fred, Hannah and Eliza had left Pickup & Co leaving Thomas to run the company alone.<ref name=WC_Museum/>

The brothers expanded into Manchester, and in 1924 created a new soft drink, that they called ''Pickups Appetizer'', which Fred use to deliver in the streets of the city in stone bottles.<ref name=MEN/> In 1931, a new company, ''Radiant Table Waters'', were formed by the Pickups in Bristol to expand the business with a home delivery service, while in 1933 ''Tizer Co. Ltd'' was set up to expand the business into London.<ref name=WC_Museum/> In 1936, ''Tizer Ltd'' was incorporated as a public company to take over the operations of F. Pickup, Pickup & Co, Tizer Co. Ltd and Radiant Table Waters.<ref name=WC_Museum/><ref>{{cite book|title=The Stock Exchange Official Year-book|date=1963|publisher=Thomas Skinner & Company|page=3168}}</ref>

=== After World War II ===

In 1956, Pickup announced that the company had made a profit of £270,209 in 1955 and that it had purchased the company, Our Boys Mineral Water based in South Wales.<ref>{{cite periodical|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_food-manufacture_1956-05-01_31_5/mode/1up?q=%22tizer+ltd%22|title=Tizer expansion|periodical=Food Manufacture|volume=31|issue=5|date=1 May 1956|page=212}}</ref> However, a year later profits had fallen to £68,818 after sales were affected by bad weather that summer.<ref>{{cite periodical|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_food-manufacture_1957-04-01_32_4/page/183/mode/1up?q=%22tizer+ltd%22|title=Rain checks Tizer Profits|periodical=Food Manufacture|volume=32|issue=4|date=1 April 1956|page=184}}</ref> The company introduced a new drink, Jusoda, which with continued improved sales in Tizer, had seen the company's profits grow to £254,196 in 1957.<ref>{{cite periodical|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_food-manufacture_1958-07-01_33_7/mode/1up?q=%22tizer+ltd%22|title=New drink well received|periodical=Food Manufacture|volume=33|issue=7|date=1 July 1958|page=306}}</ref> Thomas Pickup died in 1960,<ref name=WC_Museum/> while Fred Pickup stood down as chairman in 1962, but remained on the board until his death in 1968.<ref name=bbp>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/britishbusinessp0000stop/page/15/mode/1up?q=%22tizer+ltd%22|title=A Casebook. British business policy|author1=John M Stopford|author2=Derek F Channon|author3=David Norburn|date=1975|publisher=Macmillan Press|sbn=333-17718-5|page=1-22}}</ref> In 1960, profits after tax stood at £263,403, but as the table below shows, after a climb in profits, these had decreased by the end of the decade:<ref name=bbp/>

Tizer's chairman, F. Hindle, stated in his 1970 statement that sales had been hit by the increasing market push by the American cola companies, and as such they had agreed a licence to produce [[RC Cola|Royal Crown Cola]] in the UK.<ref name=bbp/>

To stem the losses, the company recruited a Peter Quinn, a general manager at Polyfoil Ltd, an subsidiary of Alcan, as chief executive. He noted upon his arrival in February 1970, the outdated machinery, poor marketing, un-trained managers and the localised organisation of what was by then a national business with 4% of the soft drinks market.<ref name=bbp/> Quinn started a reorganisation of the company's operations, including bringing in new managers and closing loss making or smaller depots, and introducing a new national marketing campaign developed by [[Terence Conran|Conran Design]]. Another first was producing Tizer in ring-pull cans instead of the returnable bottles. Quinn believed that the company could grow sales by 20% per annum with the changes.<ref name=bbp/>

=== New ownership ===

The company's transformation had seen sales grow to £3.551m in 1971, up from £2.949m in 1969, but there was a trading loss of £111,111.<ref name=bbp/> However in December 1971, Armour Trust, a British investment organisation, who were involved in consumer finance, property and advertising, purchased the company for £2.3m, with major shareholders such as [[Slater Walker]] accepting the offer.<ref name=bbp/> Armour quickly reversed many of Quinn's changes by reverting back to local management, selling off property and closing depots to try and stem the losses.<ref name=bbp/> Peter Quinn resigned from the company and was replaced by Michael Thomas.<ref>{{cite periodical|url=https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=EkdWAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Tizer+Ltd%22&dq=%22Tizer+Ltd%22&hl=en&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&source=gb_mobile_search&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwiQgPG1x5WUAxVGXEEAHSp8IYM4ChDoAXoECA4QAw#%22Tizer%20Ltd%22|title=Appointments|magazine=Food Processing Industry|volume=41|date=1972|page=17}}</ref>

However, Armour Trust only owned the company for a year and one day, and sold the business to Scottish drinks company [[A.G. Barr]] plc for £2.5m ($5.8 million) in December 1972.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=nhQeAQAAIAAJ&q=tizer+ltd+bought+by+armour+trust&dq=tizer+ltd+bought+by+armour+trust&hl=en&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&source=gb_mobile_search&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwiEn7aYqI6UAxV1T0EAHcHhGtoQ6AF6BAgPEAM#%22armour%20trust%22|title=A.G.Barr & Company|magazine=The Food Institute's Weekly Digest|volume=79|publisher=American Institute of Food Distribution|date=1972|page=2}}</ref><ref name=bbp/> This saw the company return to family ownership, as Fred and Thomas Pickup were nephews to William Snodgrass Barr, the grandfather of the current chairman.<ref name=Herald/> In 1973, after 6 months of development, Barr's chemists introduced a new recipe trying to re-create the original formula as close as possible.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/travel/destinations/uk-travel/england/london-travel/old-fashioned-pop-rides-nostalgia-bubble-led-by-tizer-the-appetiser-qh3sp95mm7r|title=Old fashioned pop rides nostalgia bubble led by Tizer the appetiser|newspaper=The Times|date=17 March 2007}}</ref>

In 2007, Tizer was re-branded with the slogan "Original Great Taste" and a classic recipe with fewer additives and no [[E numbers]]. It was also given classic 1976 style packaging.<ref name=MEN/> However, despite the relaunch's focus of the addition of real fruit juice and the absence of artificial flavourings, colourings and sweeteners, in 2009 the recipe was returned to the original to remove the real fruit juice and reintroduce artificial flavourings, artificial colours and sweeteners ([[Acesulfame-K]]). Tizer was rebranded in 2011 with a new logo and the slogan "The Great British Pop".<ref name=MEN/>

== Tizer variations ==
=== Tizer Ice ===
Tizer Ice was launched in the late 1990s.  The drink included [[menthol]], giving it the sensation of tasting cold, even at room temperature. Whilst known as Tizer Ice, the mascot of the drink was a variation of Ed the Tizer Head. Its sole video advertisement which was shown in [[movie theatre|cinemas]] featured a character known as the "Iceman".<ref>''AG Barr 1875–2001'' book</ref>

A 1999 print advertisement which showed children with their faces pressed against a glass surface with the slogan "How many kids can you get in your fridge?" was criticised as "inappropriate" by the [[Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents]], which had recorded deaths of children trapped inside refrigerators.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Sick+'kids+in+the+fridge'+advert+horror.-a060198375 |title=Sick 'kids in the fridge' advert horror. – Free Online Library |publisher=Thefreelibrary.com |date=13 June 1999 |accessdate=1 August 2011}}</ref> The drink was re-branded as Ice by Tizer' but poor sales saw the drink discontinued.<ref name=MEN/>

=== Tizer Diet ===
Tizer Diet was a short-lived [[low-calorie]] alternative to Tizer, originally sold in the late 1980s when known as Sugar Free Tizer, and again from 1997 to 2001 as Tizer Diet. Its 2001 advertising campaign included a bus shelter advertisement in the form of a [[curved mirror|funhouse mirror]] bearing the Tizer Diet logo, designed to make the viewer appear thinner.<ref>{{cite web|author=Diet Tizer: Mirror |url=http://www.coloribus.com/adsarchive/prints/diet-tizer-mirror-2856805/ |title="Mirror" Print ad for Diet Tizer by Bdh\tbwa |publisher=Coloribus.com |accessdate=1 August 2011}}</ref><ref name=MEN/>

===Other Tizer variants===
Barr launched several other flavour variants. In 2003, Purple and Green versions of the drink were launched, while a year later Tizer Fruitz was launched.<ref name=MEN/>

==Branding and packaging==
==="Ize" campaign===
In 1985, Tizer initiated a television campaign on [[TV-am]] exploring the "Tize-izer" vocabulary, depicting scenarios in which characters place "ize" between the syllables of words.<ref name="ED">{{cite journal |title=Sovle the Tizer Tease |journal=Evening Dispatch |date=22 August 1985 |page=7 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1180473425/?match=1&terms=tizer%20ize%20got%20the%20ize |access-date=21 May 2025 |location=Durham}}</ref> A free, promotional [[flexidisc]], featuring the voice of ''[[Spitting Image]]'' impressionist [[Rory Bremner]], was produced as part of the campaign. The ''Evening Dispatch'' described Bremner as "doing the most to help people master the new language."<ref name="ED" /> The [[tongue twister]]-based language grew in popularity among children who, according to ''[[Isle of Wight County Press]]'', would use the patois "to the complete bewilderment of mums and dads".<ref>{{cite journal |title=A Personal Stereo Is First Prize |journal=Isle of Wight County Press |date=6 September 1985 |page=40 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1075472841/?match=1&terms=tizer%20ize%20got%20the%20ize |access-date=21 May 2025}}</ref>

===Fan club===
A Tizer fan club for United Kingdom based consumers was launched in July 1991. The fan club was advertised in teenage magazines such as ''[[Smash Hits]]'' and cost £3.00 to join. In return the fan club member received a membership card and Tizer merchandise including a folder, stickers and Tizer branded wraparound sunglasses. The fan club was discontinued around 1993.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Tizer Club |url=https://tizerclub.wordpress.com/the-tizer-club/ |website=The Tizer Club|date=14 April 2020 }}</ref>

=== ---tizer campaign ===

In April 1993, Tizer launched a £2.5 million television and cinema campaign, created by the agency BDH and Partners, which aimed the product at the 16–24 age group, rather than younger children.<ref name="Patrick 1993">{{cite journal |last1=Patrick |first1=Margaret |title=Tizer's back in town as BDH wins Barr account |journal=Manchester Evening News: Mwdia |date=14 April 1993 |page=4 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/913664121/?match=1&terms=tizer%20bdh |access-date=21 May 2025}}</ref> The novel campaign, which aimed for [[cult following|cult]] status and [[credibility]], began with eight quirky television advertisements that the ''[[Manchester Evening News]]'' described as "completely off the wall".<ref name="Patrick 1993" /> The word "Tizer" was never mentioned on air; instead, each commercial utilised a [[play-on-words]], using parts of words that have "-tizer" as a suffix, such as "Bap-", "Adver-" and "Hypno-".<ref name="Patrick 1993" /> As the prefix is left on screen, the viewer is left to add the missing word "Tizer" to decipher the theme.<ref name="Manchester 1994">{{cite journal |title=More canny creations from adver-Tizer |journal=Manchester Evening News |date=4 May 1994 |page=60 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/914989665/?match=1&terms=tizer%20%20parrot |access-date=21 May 2025}}</ref> Each advert featured surreal representations and demonstrations of their respective classifications, such as raving young people and bottle jugglers; the actors – which BDH hired after scouting nightclubs in Manchester and London – appear in black-and-white against the bubbling red Tizer backdrop.<ref name="Patrick 1993" /> BDH marketing manager believed that this "brave advertising approach" would help Tizer stand out against rivals like [[Tango (drink)|Tango]], [[Lilt]], [[Coca-Cola]], [[Pepsi]] and fellow Barr product [[Irn-Bru]].<ref name="Patrick 1993" />

The advertisements proved popular enough that BDH created a further seven, "even more anarchic" advertisements, debuting in May 1994 and running throughout the summer, in a £2 million extension of the campaign. New prefixes included "stigma-", "priva-" and "dogma-", with the unusual characters and scenarios used to express each term ranging from a [[beauty queen]] sipping a can of Tizer and conceding that she's "in it for the money", an obnoxious parrot who gives out parental orders, a "veggie militant", and a bulldog informing a crowd of dogs that "poop existed before pavements."<ref name="Patrick 1993" />

===In store and incentives===

Tizer was sold at the discontinued pizza restaurant chain, [[Pizzaland]]. In 1995, cans of Tizer offered that the specific can was "worth £1 at [[Pizzaland]]" when £4 or more was spent.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://canmuseum.com/Detail.aspx?CanID=18381|title=TIZER-Lemon soda-330mL-THIS CAN IS WORTH L1-Great Britain-1995|website=Can Museum|access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref>

=== Refresh your head ===
In 1996, Tizer was rebranded, and the cans and bottles were redesigned to feature a new logo and a head mascot. The cans were changed from red to blue, and the old motto "The appetizer" was replaced by "Refresh your head". The changes by 
Pilot Design of Leeds were to appeal to the 5 to 15-year-olds core market, who thought the previous packaging was old fashioned. DJ [[Chris Evans (presenter)|Chris Evans]] fronted a £2 million TV advertising campaign to relaunch the new design.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/week-design-shake-up-tizer/62468|title=THIS WEEK: Design shake-up for Tizer|magazine=Campaign|date=24 October 1996}}</ref>

===Sponsorship===

In 1997, Tizer took over the sponsorship of ''[[The Chart Show]]'' which was a Saturday morning music chart show on the [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] network in the UK.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://uk.themedialeader.com/tizer-to-sponsor-chart-show/|title=Tizer To Sponsor Chart Show|magazine=The Media Leader|date=29 April 1997}}</ref>

From 23 January 1999, Tizer was the sponsor of the newly rebranded ''[[CD:UK]]'' which was the replacement for ''The Chart Show'' back in 1998.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://uk.themedialeader.com/tizer-to-sponsor-itvs-cduk/|title=Tizer To Sponsor ITV’s CD:UK|magazine=The Media Leader|date=15 January 1999}}</ref>

Tizer sponsored a [[roller coaster]] in [[Southport]] called the "Traumatizer" from 1999. The ride was closed in 2006 and relocated to [[Blackpool Pleasure Beach]], where it became known as "[[Infusion (roller coaster)|Infusion]]".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/news/6131902.watson-puts-fizz-in-to-pleasureland/|title=Watson puts fizz in to Pleasureland|newspaper=The Bolton News|date=3 March 1999}}</ref>

=== Lunchboxes ===

A campaign for Tizer from 2001 saw the brand package four bottles of the drink in blue lunchboxes. This was inspired by the [[Tango (drink)|Tango]] lunchbox in 2000.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/tizer-kids-lunchbox-multi-pack-run/91495|title=Tizer after kids with lunchbox multi-pack run|magazine=Campaign|date=17 September 2001}}</ref>

=== Itz a red thing ===

In 2003, a rebranding by Barr saw the company changed back to red packaging, axing its ''Refresh your head'' strapline in favour of ''Itz a red thing''. The rebrand, which cost £1.5 million, included TV adverts featuring animation by Pete Candeland, but saw the product end its sponsorship of the Saturday morning TV show CD:UK as part of its  plan to reposition the drink in the marketplace.<ref name=camp>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/tizer-aims-15m-rebrand-work-young-teenagers/195333|title=Tizer aims £1.5m rebrand work at young teenagers|magazine=Campaign|date=13 November 2003}}</ref>

=== Chameleon ===

In 2004, Tizer aired a campaign depicting a red [[chameleon]] remaining the same colour despite a number of different coloured backgrounds—the campaign's slogan was "No, we're not changing colour."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/chameleon-refuses-change-colour-tizer-campaign/213384|title=Chameleon refuses to change colour in Tizer campaign|magazine=Campaign|date=9 June 2004}}</ref>
